On Gmail spam filtering: one user found it frustrating that Google already seems to block mail from relatively new domains, yet obvious spam messages still get through.

A user who had just been complaining about the Gmail web app's interface hoped a real Gmail API would let developers build better interfaces on top, to improve inbox management and cut time spent sifting through email.

Gmail doesn't implement IMAP properly: IDLE only signals new messages, not changes in unread count. After moving from self-hosted Dovecot, the user was shocked that read status didn't propagate across devices until a manual poll.

A developer spent a year trying to replicate Gmail's interface in a desktop app (BetterInbox) over IMAP and said IMAP is completely unsuited to the Gmail paradigm. The new API would have made their lives much easier.

One developer's IMAP client code for Google Apps Gmail was 'full of hacks to convert internal ids to Gmail ids and format conversion issues'. They welcomed replacing it with a couple of HTTP calls via the Gmail API.
A user is very reluctant to give any third party access to their Gmail mailbox, because most sites allow password reset by email, so it's like handing over the keys to the castle.
Gmail API auth scopes already allow read-only access, but one user wants to restrict apps to a specific label or subfolder for better security without forwarding mail.
SMS Backup+ to Gmail has been 'fantastic for archiving all of my texts'. Each message is stored with the contact as sender, and the user can search everything relatively easily.
Workaround for Google's OAuth restrictions: GSuite admins can whitelist existing apps. The user did this for SMS Backup+ so it keeps working, but noted consumer Gmail users probably lack that option.
Facing Google's restrictions on third-party apps, one user stopped backing up to Google and instead synced SMS Backup to a local Dovecot IMAP server. Setup turned out to be incredibly simple.
A user said Google restricting seamless third-party integrations hurts utility and was 'just another reason I'm happy with moving my primary mail to FastMail on my own domain.'
Google lets anyone register my gmail address as their 'alternative recovery email' without confirmation, so I periodically get a dozen 'recover your account' emails from strangers' accounts.

A user with a fairly generic gmail address has hundreds of accounts linked to it that they never signed up for, because people mistype or don't know their own address. The account became unusable, so they switched to their own domain about a decade ago.
